certificationCard.description: The developer-track credential from Anthropic. Unlike theory-heavy certifications, the CCDV-F measures whether you can actually ship AI-powered features — calling the Messages API, routing between models, chaining tools, streaming responses, handling errors gracefully, and writing evaluation harnesses that catch regressions before users do.

keyConcepts.h2: Claude Certified Developer: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Building Applications on the Messages API
blocks.body: A third of the exam lives here. You need to know how to structure a Messages API call — system prompt, conversation history, max tokens, temperature — and what comes back. The exam tests real integration decisions: when to use streaming vs. batch responses, how to handle rate limits and retries, how to pass images alongside text, and how to parse structured JSON output from Claude. Expect questions that give you a code snippet and ask what happens when you change one parameter.

blocks.heading: Prompt Engineering for Production Systems
blocks.body: This isn't the same as casual prompting. The CCDV-F tests techniques that matter in code: XML-tagged input sections so Claude can parse structured data, system prompts that enforce output schemas, few-shot examples embedded programmatically, and chain-of-thought reasoning triggered by instruction rather than hope. You also need to handle prompt injection defenses — making sure user-supplied text can't override your system instructions.

blocks.heading: Working with the SDK and Authentication
blocks.body: Questions cover the Python and TypeScript SDKs: initializing the client, managing API keys without hardcoding them, setting up retries and timeouts, and switching between model versions. The exam assumes you know the difference between the raw HTTP API and the SDK wrapper, and can debug common issues — wrong content type, malformed message arrays, exceeding context windows.

blocks.heading: Tool Use, Function Calling, and Agents
blocks.body: Fifteen percent of the exam focuses on giving Claude the ability to call your functions. You define tools with JSON schemas, Claude decides when to invoke them and with what arguments, your code runs the function and returns the result, and Claude incorporates that result into its response. The exam tests the full loop — schema definition, argument validation, error handling when a tool fails, and multi-turn agents that chain several tool calls to complete a task.

blocks.heading: Testing and Evaluating AI Applications
blocks.body: The final domain covers how you know your AI feature actually works. Expect questions on writing eval datasets, measuring response quality with automated graders, tracking regression across model updates, and A/B testing prompt variants. The exam also tests your understanding of when to use human evaluation vs. model-based evaluation, and how to build a feedback loop that improves prompts over time.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Claude Certified Developer Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The CCDV-F is a hands-on certification. If you have built something real with the Claude API — even a side project — you already have most of what you need. If you haven't, build one before you sit the exam.

blocks.heading: Build a Working Project Before You Study
blocks.body: Pick a real problem — a Slack bot that summarizes channels, a CLI that reviews pull requests, a web app that answers questions from uploaded PDFs — and build it end-to-end with the Claude API. You will encounter rate limits, context-window overflows, flaky JSON parsing, and tool-call edge cases. Those encounters teach more than any study guide.

blocks.heading: Know the API Parameters Cold
blocks.body: Temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop_sequences, system prompt placement — the exam expects you to predict how changing each one affects output. Set up a test harness and experiment: what happens at temperature 0 vs. 1? What does top_p do when combined with temperature? When does max_tokens truncate mid-sentence vs. mid-word?

blocks.heading: Practice the Tool-Use Loop
blocks.body: Define three or four tools, wire them up, and run multi-turn conversations where Claude calls them. Pay attention to what happens when a tool returns an error, when Claude calls a tool with invalid arguments, and when the conversation needs multiple sequential tool calls to reach an answer. Those failure modes are exam favorites.

blocks.heading: Write At Least One Eval Suite
blocks.body: Create a spreadsheet of input-output pairs for your project. Run them through your prompt automatically and score the results. Change the prompt, rerun, compare. This workflow is exactly what the evaluation domain tests — and doing it once makes those questions trivial.

blocks.heading: Read the Official Documentation
blocks.body: Anthropic's docs at docs.anthropic.com are the exam's source of truth. Read the prompt engineering guide, the tool use guide, and the API reference at least once. The exam does not test obscure trivia, but it does test whether you know the documented best practices vs. common antipatterns.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Certifications After Claude Developer
nextCertsAfter.intro: After earning the Developer credential, move into architecture-level certifications:

sampleQuestions.question: You are building a customer support chatbot that needs to look up order status in your database. Which Claude feature enables this?
options: Setting a higher temperature so Claude can guess order statuses more creatively
Defining a tool with a JSON schema for the lookup function, letting Claude call it mid-conversation and incorporating the returned data into its response
Pasting the entire orders database into the system prompt
Using a fine-tuned model trained on your order data
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tool use lets Claude call external functions when it needs data it doesn't have. You define the tool schema, Claude decides when to call it, and your code executes the actual database query and returns the result.

sampleQuestions.question: Your API call returns a 529 status code. What does this indicate and what should you do?
options: The API key is invalid — generate a new one
The request payload is malformed — check your JSON structure
Anthropic's API is temporarily overloaded — implement exponential backoff and retry after a delay
Your account has been suspended — contact support
sampleQuestions.explanation: A 529 means the API is temporarily overloaded. The correct response is exponential backoff with retries. This is different from a 429 (rate limit), which means your account specifically is sending too many requests.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the primary risk of including user-supplied text directly in the system prompt without sanitization?
options: It increases API costs because system prompts are billed at a higher rate
User input could contain instructions that override your system prompt, causing Claude to ignore your intended behavior (prompt injection)
The system prompt has a strict 100-token limit that user text would exceed
User text in system prompts causes Claude to switch languages automatically
sampleQuestions.explanation: Prompt injection occurs when untrusted user input is placed where Claude treats it as instructions. User-supplied text should go in user messages, not system prompts, and system prompts should include explicit instructions to ignore any override attempts in user input.

sampleQuestions.question: You want Claude to always return a specific JSON structure with fields 'summary', 'sentiment', and 'confidence'. What is the most reliable approach?
options: Ask nicely in the user message: 'please return JSON'
Define the exact schema in the system prompt with an example, set temperature to 0, and parse the response with error handling for cases where the format is not followed
Set max_tokens to exactly the number of characters in your expected JSON
Use a regular expression to extract JSON from any response
sampleQuestions.explanation: Reliable structured output requires a clear schema definition in the system prompt, low temperature for consistency, and defensive parsing in your code. Relying on a polite request or regex extraction is fragile in production.

sampleQuestions.question: When should you use streaming responses instead of waiting for the complete response?
options: Always — streaming is faster and cheaper in every scenario
When building interactive UIs where users expect to see text appear progressively, reducing perceived latency on long responses
Only when the response will be exactly 100 tokens
Never — streaming adds unnecessary complexity
sampleQuestions.explanation: Streaming is most valuable in user-facing applications where perceived latency matters. Users see the first tokens within milliseconds instead of waiting seconds for a complete response. For background batch jobs, the added complexity of handling streaming events may not be worth it.

sampleQuestions.question: Your Claude-powered feature worked well with claude-sonnet-4-20250514 but produces worse results after switching to a newer model version. What is the recommended approach?
options: Immediately revert to the old model and never update
Run your existing eval suite against the new model, identify which test cases regressed, adjust prompts if needed, and only deploy the new model when evals pass
Assume the new model is always better and deploy without testing
File a bug report and wait for Anthropic to fix the model
sampleQuestions.explanation: Model updates can shift behavior in ways that affect specific use cases. An eval suite catches regressions before they reach users. If some evals fail, the prompt may need adjustment for the new model's strengths — blind rollback or blind deployment both carry risk.

sampleQuestions.question: What happens when a conversation exceeds the model's context window?
options: Claude automatically summarizes older messages to make room
The API returns an error — your application needs to handle truncation, summarization, or conversation splitting before sending the request
Claude silently ignores the oldest messages
The API automatically charges for additional context capacity
sampleQuestions.explanation: The API does not silently truncate or auto-summarize. When a request exceeds the context window, it fails. Your application must manage conversation length — common strategies include summarizing older turns, dropping system-less messages, or starting a new conversation with a summary.

sampleQuestions.question: You need to process 10,000 support tickets through Claude for classification. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Send all 10,000 in a single API call as one massive prompt
Use the Batches API to submit all requests at once and retrieve results when processing completes, getting a 50% cost discount
Process them one at a time in a synchronous loop with no error handling
Copy and paste each ticket into Claude.ai manually
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Batches API is designed for high-volume, non-interactive workloads. It processes requests asynchronously, handles queuing internally, and offers a 50% cost reduction compared to real-time API calls. Single-call approaches fail on context limits, and synchronous loops are slow and fragile.

sampleQuestions.question: A developer stores their Anthropic API key directly in the source code and pushes it to a public GitHub repository. What are the immediate risks?
options: No risk — API keys in source code are a standard practice
Anyone who finds the repository can use the key to make API calls billed to the developer's account, and bots actively scan public repositories for leaked keys
The key automatically expires when pushed to GitHub
GitHub blocks all commits containing API keys
sampleQuestions.explanation: Leaked API keys are exploited within minutes — automated scanners constantly search public repositories. The key should be stored in environment variables or a secrets manager, and the compromised key should be rotated immediately via the Anthropic console.

sampleQuestions.question: When defining a tool for Claude, what makes a good tool description?
options: Keep it as short as possible — one word is ideal

Include a clear explanation of what the tool does, when to use it, what each parameter means, and what the return value contains — Claude uses this description to decide whether and how to call the tool
Write the description in a programming language Claude understands
Leave the description empty and let Claude figure out the tool's purpose from its name
sampleQuestions.explanation: Claude relies on tool descriptions to decide when a tool is relevant and how to call it correctly. A thorough description with parameter semantics and usage guidance produces better tool-selection accuracy than a terse or missing description.
